prize_parts.citation: for a visionary, densely patterned Romanian-language oeuvre, centred on its large prose architectures and grounded in poetry, in which memory, the body and dream are built into an inner cosmos

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: one writer, Mircea Cărtărescu (B011), in one prize part. What changed in round 2 is the citation wording, which I have moved from 'prose and poetry' to a prose-centred text that names the poetry as the ground of the oeuvre. Round 1 showed that Olsson, Carlberg and Sem-Sandberg all put the weight on the large prose works, and none of us can show that the poetry carries a separate case. On the common criteria, as I understand them from public knowledge, the case is this. The voice is recognisable as his alone. The Orbitor sequence (Blinding is its first volume) and Solenoid read as a single metaphysical project that treats memory, the body and dream as one imaginative system. The architecture appears cumulative rather than merely long. The achievement is a distinctive imaginative and formal one, not a topical or occasional one. The major structures are published, so the oeuvre can be assessed now, and attribution is clean. I rest the case on the written work and its internal design, not on the fact that all six openings agree. That agreement tells us nothing about merit, and the chair's questions show it has not yet been tested against the late volumes. I also see no literary ground in the exchange to prefer P000. The reservations are about verification and translation. They are not findings that the work falls short.
statement.case_against: The reservation that matters most is still unresolved, and round 1 did not resolve it. It is whether the later volumes advance the project or only enlarge it. I cannot name specific volumes as evidence of development without claiming a knowledge of the text that I do not have. Olsson's reading that the late work extends the earlier project is plausible. Mattson-the-reader, working from public knowledge, can accept it only provisionally. Second, so much of the claim rests on sentence-level density and rhythm in Romanian that the committee's judgment of style is indirect. Third, the poetry and early work are thinly covered in translation, so any weight the citation gives them is unsupported. Fourth, a prose-centred citation concedes that the whole-oeuvre claim is carried by the novels, and that is a narrower claim than the one I made in round 1. If Romanian-reading expert reports showed repetition or loss of control in the later volumes, the case would weaken. The comparison with Can Xue or Carson would then have to be reopened on the evidence, not by assumption.

responses.point: Olsson accepted my over-extension concern but asked me to separate length from loss of control. He proposed that the committee test whether the later volumes advance the project, and that the citation lean on the strongest long works if they do not.
responses.response: The distinction is fair, and I accept it. By length I mean only the number of pages and volumes, which is not a defect. By loss of control I would mean specific things: motifs recurring without transformation, a structural design no longer governing the material, or a sentence-level density that becomes mannered. I cannot point to a specific volume as showing either, and I will not pretend to. I therefore take his fallback as the right drafting rule. The citation should rest on the large prose works, with the poetry named as ground, so it does not depend on an unverified judgment about every late volume. That is my reason for changing the wording. I agree with his condition that the poetry carries weight only if it can be shown to.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg said he would hold the claim that the late work extends the earlier project as provisional. He also said he wants a concrete argument for development within Can Xue's mode before ranking her above Cărtărescu.
responses.response: I share both positions, and I need to be candid that I cannot supply the argument he asks for on Can Xue. I ranked her third in my opening, and my round 1 said I could not confirm sustained development in her work. The exchange has not changed that. I would not claim to know which of her works deepen the dream-logic mode. His wish for evidence on her is legitimate, but the same standard has to apply to Cărtărescu. Our confidence that his late work extends the project is also provisional. What distinguishes the two cases is that Cărtărescu's multi-volume structure at least offers visible stages we can discuss. That is a difference in the evidence, not a finding about quality. I agree with his view that Romanian-reading expert reports would do more than another round of ranking.

responses.point: Sward said her reason for placing Can Xue behind Cărtărescu is an asymmetry of evidence, not a different estimate of quality. She added that she would compare the two if unevenness in the late Cărtărescu volumes proved real.
responses.response: I agree with the conditional, and her framing is more honest than a bare ranking. I would add one caution. An asymmetry of evidence is a reason for care, not a literary argument for the candidate we know better. If the translated corpus of Can Xue is thin, that limits our confidence in her case. It does not lower her case. I am glad she has named what would reopen the comparison. I would add a second trigger: Romanian-reading evidence that the late novels repeat the earlier project would also have to be taken seriously. Without either trigger I keep Cărtărescu first. I treat Can Xue as my leading alternative because her singularity of method is not in doubt, and the open question is development, which none of us can currently answer.

responses.point: Palm treats the classification of Carson's hybrid works as a drafting difficulty more than a literary weakness. She also pointed out that the Cărtărescu translation limit cannot be resolved by discussion alone.
responses.response: On Carson I partly agree. The formal invention of Autobiography of Red and Nox is a literary strength, and her English can be judged directly, which is a real advantage. I would not dismiss the classification problem as only drafting, though. If translations and adaptations were set aside, the original core might be narrower than the best-known books suggest. That bears on sustained quality across the oeuvre, which is why she stays an alternative for me and not my first choice. I accept her point on translation. Discussion cannot settle it, and the useful step is outside input, such as Romanian readers or the best Swedish translations, not more argument among us. I keep Carson as my second alternative on the strength of the formal case.

responses.point: Carlberg proposed a prose-centred citation that names the poetry as part of the oeuvre without resting the award on it. She also treats Adonis as a strong alternative but not a firm first choice because of the limits of translating Arabic prosody.
responses.response: I adopt her proposal on the citation. It is the main reason my wording changed. On Adonis, I maintain my rank of him as an important formal case, and I agree that it must be argued from the poems themselves and not from critical influence or public positions. The chair has asked which collections could carry that argument. I cannot name a case I can assess, because the achievement lies in the very diction and prosody that translation loses. I would therefore not move him above Cărtărescu on what is before the committee, and I would revise only if Arabic-reading experts argue the case from specific collections.

uncertainties: Whether the later volumes of Cărtărescu's multi-part works advance the project or only enlarge it. I cannot settle this from public knowledge and I have not verified the later volumes.
How much of the sentence-level density and rhythm of the Romanian prose survives translation, and whether a committee reading mostly through translation over- or underrates it.
How much weight the poetry and early work can bear. The prose-centred citation reflects my inability to show this, not a finding that the poetry is weak.
Whether the dream-logic method of Can Xue deepens over the corpus or repeats, given partial translation.
Which of Carson's works count as her oeuvre if translations and adaptations are set aside, and whether the remainder supports sustained quality.
Whether Adonis can be argued from the poems without prosodic access, and how to weigh his influence against the intrinsic quality of the texts.
Whether Nobel's phrase about work of an idealistic tendency fits a metaphysical project of this kind. This is a committee interpretation, not a fact I can establish.

My judgments rest on public knowledge, not fresh reading, and I have not independently verified sources. My own public statements say a committee member can lack access to a candidate in the original, and that applies to me for every non-Swedish candidate here.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1 and no connection to any shortlisted writer is apparent from the supplied profile. The profile documents committee colleagues Olsson, Swärd, Sem-Sandberg and Palm, a shared 2019 renewal round with Swärd, and a long career as a critic in the Gothenburg and West Sweden press. None of these involves a candidate. Collegial ties are not a reason to prefer or reject any position in this exchange. My own practice as a novelist and critic is context, not evidence of a preference. This disclosure rests on my reading of the supplied profile and is not independently verified.
